assertions.value: The authors state that computing dim(g) by iterative commutator closure needs rank checks of cost O(D cubed) with D = dim(g), so for hardware-efficient ansatzes, where D can reach 4 to the n, the worst case approaches O(64 to the n), and the full HEA DLA quickly hits an exponential memory wall while the SPA's operator space stays small.

while computing the full DLA for unstructured HEAs quickly hits the exponential memory wall (O(4n) generators)

assertions.value: The authors report that over n from 2 to 10 the HEA gradient variance decays exponentially, closely following the O(1/4 to the n) scaling when deep enough, severely inhibiting trainability for n ≥ 10, while the SPA shows a polynomial decay profile; the result is shown only as a plot.

assertions.value: The authors report that the HEA generator set spans the full special unitary algebra with dimension about 4 to the n minus 1, while the SPA generator set, built on symmetry invariants such as parity or magnetization, yields a DLA growing only polynomially with n; the values are shown only as a plot.

restricts the DLA to a subspace whose dimension grows only polynomially with n

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Algorithms for Unsupervised Machine Learning and Neural Networks
papers.version_note: PhD thesis of Jonas Landman (Universite de Paris, supervised by Iordanis Kerenidis), arXiv:2111.03598v1, October 2021. 192 PDF pages; printed page numbers run 2 behind PDF page numbers in the body. The text layer drops most epsilon symbols and garbles some display equations (for example Theorems 3.4, 4.5, 8.1, 8.3 and Algorithm 1); those pages were read from the rendered page images, so the content is read in full, but quotes are cut around the lost symbols. Pages 179 to 192 are the bibliography.
papers.what_it_is: A PhD thesis that collects the author's quantum algorithms for unsupervised learning (q-means, quantum spectral clustering) and neural networks (quantum convolutional neural networks, quantum pyramidal circuits for orthogonal neural networks), with the supporting quantum subroutines (QRAM access, l-infinity tomography, distance estimation), proved running times, classical simulations of the quantum effects, and a small IBM hardware experiment.

quotes: It remains an open question to find classical algorithms for these machine learning problems that are polylogarithmic in the dimension and are competitive with respect to the quantum or the classical algorithms for the same problems.
Experimental comparisons with the usual classical algorithms have been done in [ADBL19] but don't seem in favor of the new quantum inspired algorithms.

existing.value: The author states that the thesis proves an asymptotic advantage in complexity or running time for each quantum algorithm compared with the classical case, with random effects due to the quantum computation; the algorithms give hope for an ideal quantum computer in the future, and many efforts remain in practice, from error correction to quantum data access.
quotes: We prove that these quantum algorithms are faster compared to their classical version, but exhibit random effects due to the quantum nature of the computation.
The quantum algorithms presented in this thesis give hope for the utility of an ideal quantum computer in the future.
Indeed, we prove an asymptotic advantage for each algorithm in terms of complexity or running time, compared to the classical case.
That being said, for this hope to become reality, many efforts remain to be realized in practice, from error correction to quantum data access.

existing.reader_inference: The proofs compare asymptotic step counts under QRAM access and fault tolerance; they do not establish wall-clock advantage.

assertions.value: The author shows that a quantum pyramidal circuit of RBS gates for an n by n layer has n(n - 1)/2 free parameters, exactly the number of free parameters of an n by n orthogonal matrix, with linear depth and only nearest-neighbor connectivity; restricted to the unary basis its unitary is an orthogonal matrix, so any orthogonal layer has a pyramidal circuit and vice versa.
quotes: imposes the number of free parameters to be n(n − 1)/2, the exact number of free parameters to specify a n × n orthogonal matrix.
Note finally that this circuit has linear depth and is convenient for near term quantum hardware platforms with restricted connectivity.
Therefore, for any given neural network's orthogonal layer, there is a quantum pyramidal circuit that reproduces it.
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived in Sections 12.1 and 12.2 of the thesis.

assertions.value: The author shows a fully classical, quantum-inspired training method that computes the gradients of all n(n - 1)/2 angles of a pyramidal orthogonal layer in time O(n2) while keeping the weight matrix strictly orthogonal, against the previously best-known O(n3).
quotes: the main advantage of our method is that we can also now train orthogonal weight matrices classically in time O(n2), instead of the previously best-known O(n3).
our classical algorithm allows us to compute the gradients of the n(n− 1)/2 angles in time O(n2)
assertions.certainty_reason: A complexity derivation in Section 12.3.
assertions.reader_inference: This result is classical; it needs no quantum hardware.
